answer.question: Can I put artificial turf in my Pablo Creek Reserve yard?
answer.answer: Not without ARB approval. The manual never mentions artificial turf, but landscape changes need the ARB's sign-off before installation, and a set share of each yard stays in shrubs and ground cover. Ask in writing first.

blocks.h2: Nothing changes in the yard until the ARB stamps it.
blocks.takeaway: Nothing in the yard changes until the ARB approves it, and the manual doesn't name artificial turf directly. Ask which category your plan falls under before any work starts, since starting early costs more.
paras: Your yard answers to the Architectural Review Board's Standards and Procedures Manual, effective June 23, 2021, and posted as the PCR ARB Manual 2022. The ARB reviews driveways, walkways, patios and anything visible from the road or a neighboring lot, and its approval comes before permitting, construction or installation. Every hardscape change needs approval, and so does a moderate landscape change, though that one carries no review fee.

The manual never mentions artificial turf. It lists putting greens with gazebos and pergolas as other structures, and has a separate category for major landscaping modifications. Ask the ARB, through Marsh Landing Management Company, the community's property manager, whether turf is allowed, where on the lot, and which category your plan falls under. Ask for the current edition too.
Starting early costs more than waiting. Work begun without approval doubles the processing fee, can go to the Violation Hearing Committee for a fine, and may have to come out, with the yard restored.

blocks.h2: Part of every yard stays in shrubs and ground cover.
blocks.takeaway: Your lot type sets how much of the yard must stay in shrubs and ground cover, which limits how much can become turf. We measure your yard and fit the layout into what's left over.
paras: The landscape guidelines set how much of each lot stays planted, which caps how much can become lawn of any kind. A Cottage home site keeps about one-third of the front yard and no less than 25% of the rear yard in shrubs and ground cover, counting the foundation hedge. An Estate home site keeps about 25% of the front and no less than 20% of the rear. On a Cottage lot, planting inside a screened enclosure doesn't count toward it.

The landscape plan carries a table to prove it: each yard's area, the minimum planted area and the planted area drawn. The front yard also takes in the strip between your lot line and the back of the curb.
That table is where the free visit starts. We measure each yard, mark the beds and hedges the manual requires, and fit the turf into what remains. You approve the layout before you submit it.

blocks.h2: A putting green counts as a structure. A fenced dog run isn't allowed.
blocks.takeaway: A putting green counts as a structure and stays out of easements. Fences can't create a dog run, so put pet turf in open yard where the dog already heads.
paras: Putting greens count as other structures, and the manual keeps permanent structures out of the easements your site plan must show. Golf driving nets can't be permanent and have to be moved out of view after use, so design a backyard putting green for putting and chipping, not a hitting bay.

Fences may not be used to create a dog run on any home site; the manual encourages an invisible underground fence instead. Pet turf here is a patch of open yard, not a pen, so put it where the dog already heads and a hose can reach.

Fences are open-picket wrought iron or aluminum, generally no more than 4 feet tall. That matters under Fla. Stat. 720.3045, which bars an association from restricting items, artificial turf among them, that can't be seen from the frontage, an adjacent parcel, an adjacent common area or a community golf course. A see-through fence rarely hides a yard from next door, so get the ARB's answer in writing; our Florida HOA guide covers denials.

blocks.h2: Irrigation rules written for sod, right down to the water.
blocks.takeaway: The irrigation rules were written for sod, right down to the water's edge, so ask the ARB in writing whether zones under your turf can be capped.
paras: The manual expects a fully automatic underground irrigation system on every home site, covering its landscape and turf and the banks of a lake, with rotor heads for sodded areas. Where a home site touches a lake or a Nature Reserve, you install and maintain the landscape and irrigation to the water's edge or the preserve. Irrigation may not be drawn from the lakes.

None of that was written with an artificial lawn in mind. Ask the ARB in writing whether the zones under the turf can be capped, and which beds and banks must stay watered. Expect a close look from across the water: on lake lots the manual keeps play structures beside the house, not behind it.
Watering beds from a well? Only deep, artesian wells are approved; the ARB says the iron in shallow wells can stain sidewalks and homes.

blocks.h2: Build on the grading plan, and leave the conservation areas alone.
blocks.takeaway: We build your turf base to follow the lot's approved grading plan, so rain moves the way it's designed to. Conservation areas on the plat stay untouched, so pull your plat first.
paras: The manual describes the site as sandy ridges, pine flatlands and wetland preserves. Each lot is graded to a Neighborhood Grading Plan approved by the City of Jacksonville, and we build the turf base to follow that grade, so rain leaves the lot as designed instead of pooling against a bed or running into a neighbor's yard.

Areas marked Conservation on the recorded plats fall under permits from the St. Johns River Water Management District and the Army Corps of Engineers, which prohibit construction, clearing, filling, tree cutting and removal of any vegetation there. Pull your plat before the layout is drawn.

Crews come in through a gate, and the gate access policy makes you responsible for contractors following its procedures, so ask Marsh Landing Management how a crew gets listed for entry. The Declaration is recorded in both St. Johns and Duval county records (2020 amendment); confirm which county your parcel sits in before any public permit question.

servicesNote: Compare a putting green, an open-yard pet area or a lawn within the part of your lot the planting minimums leave free.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Pablo Creek Reserve?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, backyard putting greens and pet turf in Pablo Creek Reserve, Jacksonville. The ARB manual shapes every layout here, from each yard's planted share to the ban on fenced dog runs, so we measure first and draw the turf around it. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: How long does the ARB take to decide?
faq.a: The manual has plan-review packages due to Marsh Landing Management by 2:00 PM on the Wednesday before the next scheduled ARB meeting, and says the ARB approves or disapproves, with written comments, in thirty business days at its regular meeting. Stamped plans are void if work doesn't start within 120 days. Ask whether a yard-only submittal runs on the same calendar.

faq.q: Does ARB approval cover the city's rules?
faq.a: No. The ARB's hold-harmless agreement leaves building codes, government ordinances and the Pablo Creek Reserve PUD Ordinance to you and your contractor. Our Jacksonville page covers the city's side of turf, including the watering days.

faq.q: Can turf go under the oaks?
faq.a: Plan around the roots, and ask the ARB. The manual asks that roots of preserved trees not be disturbed unnecessarily, and street and easement trees can't be removed or trimmed without approval. Under a thick canopy, a bed of shrubs and ground cover counts toward the planting minimum, leaving turf for the open yard.
